q: Which complexity class contains the problems that a deterministic algorithm can solve in polynomial time?
x: P is the class of problems solvable in polynomial time, such as O(n) or O(n²). NP-hard and NP-complete problems have no known polynomial-time algorithm, and unsolvable problems have no algorithm at all.

q: Which statement describes the class NP?
o: No algorithm can ever solve its problems
Its problems can be solved only in exponential time
It contains only problems that are not in P
A proposed solution can be checked in polynomial time
x: NP means a given answer can be verified quickly (in polynomial time), even if finding it may be hard. NP includes every problem in P, so saying it contains only problems outside P, or only exponential ones, is wrong.

q: A problem is called NP-complete when it:
o: can be solved in linear time by a simple loop
has been proved to have no algorithm at all
is in P but cannot be checked in polynomial time
is in NP and every NP problem can be reduced to it
x: NP-complete problems are the hardest problems in NP: they are themselves in NP, and every NP problem reduces to them. A problem with no algorithm at all is unsolvable, which is a different idea.

q: The halting problem (deciding for every program and input whether the program will eventually stop) is an example of:
x: It has been proved that no algorithm can decide halting for every program and input, so the problem is unsolvable (undecidable). It is not in P, because P needs an algorithm that always gives the answer.

q: Merge sort splits a list into two halves, sorts each half the same way and then combines the sorted halves. Which design technique is this?
x: Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems, solving each and combining the results is divide and conquer. A greedy method instead makes the best-looking single choice at each step without splitting the problem.

q: To pay Rs 80 with notes of Rs 50, Rs 20 and Rs 10, a cashier always picks the largest note that does not exceed the amount still to be paid. Which design technique is this?
x: Choosing the locally best option (the largest note that fits) at every step is the greedy method: 50, then 20, then 10. Divide and conquer would split the problem into independent halves, which does not happen here.

q: A program finds a forgotten 3-digit lock code by trying every code from 000 to 999 and testing each one. In the worst case, how many codes are tested?
x: From 000 to 999 there are 10 × 10 × 10 = 1000 codes, and in the worst case the right one is the last tried. 999 forgets that 000 is also a code; 900 counts only codes that do not start with 0.

q: Which of these is a decision problem (one whose answer is simply yes or no)?
o: Find the largest number in a list
Arrange a list of names alphabetically
Find the shortest road from P to Q
x: "Is 91 a prime number?" can only be answered yes or no (here no, as 91 = 7 × 13). Finding the largest number is a search problem and finding the shortest road is an optimisation problem; their answers are values, not yes or no.

q:
For a list of size `n`, what is the time complexity of this Python code?
```
count = 0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(n):
        count += 1
```
x: The inner loop runs n times for each of the n passes of the outer loop, so `count += 1` runs n × n times: O(n²). O(n) would be a single loop.

q:
What is printed?
```
n = 64
i = n
steps = 0
while i > 1:
    i = i // 2
    steps += 1
print(steps)
```
x: i goes 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, which is 6 halvings, and the loop stops when i is 1. Answering 7 counts the starting value as a step; this halving pattern is why such loops are O(log n).

q: For very large n, which of these grows the slowest?
x: log n grows far more slowly than n; for n = 1024, log₂ n is only 10. O(n²) and O(2ⁿ) grow faster than O(n), and O(2ⁿ) fastest of all.

q: Which statement about the classes P and NP is true?
o: Every problem in P is also in NP
Every problem in NP has been proved to be in P
NP-complete problems are known to have polynomial-time algorithms
It has been proved that P and NP are different
x: If a problem can be solved in polynomial time, its answer can also be checked in polynomial time, so P is inside NP. Whether P equals NP is still an open question, so the two "proved" statements are false.

q: Which of these is a well-known NP-complete problem?
o: Finding the maximum of a list
Binary search in a sorted list
x: The decision version of the travelling salesman problem (is there a tour shorter than a given length?) is NP-complete. Linear search, finding a maximum and binary search all run in polynomial time, so they are in P.

q: A set of steps works on most inputs but, for one input, keeps repeating forever without stopping. Which property of an algorithm does it fail?
x: An algorithm must end after a finite number of steps (finiteness). Definiteness means each step is clear and unambiguous; the steps here may be clear, but they never finish.

q: A generate-and-test program tries every arrangement of the four letters P, Q, R and S, each letter used exactly once, until it finds a valid one. In the worst case, how many arrangements does it test?
x: There are 4 choices for the first letter, 3 for the second, 2 for the third and 1 for the last: 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24. 256 = 4⁴ would allow letters to repeat, which the stem rules out.

q:
What is printed?
```
total = 0
for i in range(1, 5):
    for j in range(i):
        total += 1
print(total)
```
x: i takes 1, 2, 3, 4 (5 is excluded) and the inner loop runs i times, so total = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. 16 assumes the inner loop runs 4 times each pass; 15 wrongly includes i = 5.

q: Binary search can be used only when the list is:
x: Binary search compares with the middle element and discards half the list, which works only if the list is in order. Duplicates and odd or even length do not stop it.

q: What is the worst-case time complexity of linear search on a list of n items?
x: In the worst case linear search checks every one of the n items, so it is O(n). O(log n) is binary search on a sorted list.

q: Bubble sort (ascending) goes left to right and swaps each adjacent pair whose left value is larger. What is the list after the first full pass on `[5, 1, 4, 2, 8]`?
x: 5,1 swap → [1, 5, 4, 2, 8]; 5,4 swap → [1, 4, 5, 2, 8]; 5,2 swap → [1, 4, 2, 5, 8]; 5,8 no swap. One pass only moves the largest value to the end, so the list is not yet fully sorted.

q: Bubble sort (ascending) goes left to right in each pass and swaps each adjacent pair whose left value is larger. What is the list after the first two full passes on `[6, 3, 5, 1, 2]`?
Selection sort (ascending): each pass finds the smallest value in the unsorted part and swaps it with the first unsorted position. What is `[29, 10, 14, 37, 13]` after two passes?
x: Pass 1: smallest is 10, swap with 29 → [10, 29, 14, 37, 13]. Pass 2: smallest of 29, 14, 37, 13 is 13, swap with 29 → [10, 13, 14, 37, 29]. [10, 29, 14, 37, 13] is after one pass only.

q: Insertion sort (ascending) takes each element from the left and inserts it into its place in the sorted part before it. Starting with `[4, 3, 2, 10, 12, 1]`, what is the list just after the value 2 has been inserted?
x: Insert 3 before 4 → [3, 4, 2, 10, 12, 1]; insert 2 before 3 → [2, 3, 4, 10, 12, 1]. The values to the right of 2 have not been touched yet, so 1 is still last.

q: Binary search looks for 41 in `[3, 8, 12, 17, 21, 25, 30, 41, 50]` (indexes 0 to 8), using middle index = (low + high) // 2. Which values are compared with 41, in order?
x: low 0, high 8, mid 4 → 21 < 41, so low = 5; mid (5 + 8) // 2 = 6 → 30 < 41, so low = 7; mid (7 + 8) // 2 = 7 → 41 found. Three comparisons: 21, 30, 41.

q: Binary search looks for 17 in `[2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]` (indexes 0 to 7), using middle index = (low + high) // 2 and stopping when low > high. How many list elements are compared with 17?
x: mid 3 → 8, low = 4; mid 5 → 12, low = 6; mid 6 → 14, low = 7; mid 7 → 16, low = 8 > high 7, so the search stops: 4 comparisons. 8 would be linear search checking every element.

q: Linear search starts at the first element of `[7, 3, 14, 9, 14]` and stops at the first match. How many comparisons does it make when searching for 14?
x: It compares 7, then 3, then 14, and stops at the third comparison. 5 would mean it went on to the last 14, but linear search stops at the first match.

q: About how many comparisons does binary search need, in the worst case, to search a sorted list of 1000 elements?
x: Each comparison halves the list: 1000 → 500 → 250 → … → 1 takes about 10 steps, since 2¹⁰ = 1024. 1000 comparisons is the worst case for linear search.

q: Which sorting method repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are in the wrong order?
x: Bubble sort works by swapping adjacent out-of-order pairs, so large values "bubble" to the end. Selection sort instead picks the smallest remaining value and swaps it into place.

q: A bubble sort makes a pass of adjacent comparisons and stops as soon as a pass makes no swaps. How many comparisons does it make on the already sorted list `[2, 4, 6, 8, 9]`?
x: The first pass compares the 4 adjacent pairs (2,4), (4,6), (6,8), (8,9), makes no swap, and the sort stops. 10 is the count for all four passes without the early stop.

q: A bubble sort on 5 elements always makes 4 passes, and pass k makes 5 − k comparisons. How many comparisons does it make in total?
x: The passes make 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons. 16 assumes every pass compares all 4 pairs; 25 is 5 × 5.

q: What is the time complexity of merge sort on a list of n elements?
x: Merge sort halves the list about log n times and merging at each level takes about n steps, giving O(n log n). O(n²) is the worst case of bubble, selection and insertion sort.

q: Selection sort (ascending): each pass finds the smallest value in the unsorted part and swaps it with the first unsorted position (a value already in place stays). What is `[5, 2, 9, 1, 6]` after three passes?
x: Pass 1: 1 swaps with 5 → [1, 2, 9, 5, 6]. Pass 2: smallest of 2, 9, 5, 6 is 2, already in place. Pass 3: smallest of 9, 5, 6 is 5, swap with 9 → [1, 2, 5, 9, 6]. [1, 2, 9, 5, 6] is after two passes.

q: A list of n values is already in ascending order. Which of these takes about n steps (O(n)) to sort it?
o: Bubble sort that always makes all n − 1 passes
x: On a sorted list insertion sort compares each new element once with the one before it and moves nothing, so it takes O(n). Selection sort still scans the whole unsorted part every pass (O(n²)), and merge sort is O(n log n) on any input.
The loop checks index 0 (4), then index 1 (9), which matches, and `return i` ends the function at once with 1. 3 would be the last 9, but the function never gets there.

q:
What is printed?
```
nums = [5, 2, 8, 1]
for i in range(len(nums) - 1):
    if nums[i] > nums[i + 1]:
        nums[i], nums[i + 1] = nums[i + 1], nums[i]
print(nums)
```
x: i runs 0, 1, 2: 5 > 2 swap → [2, 5, 8, 1]; 5 > 8 no; 8 > 1 swap → [2, 5, 1, 8]. This is a single bubble-sort pass, so the list is not fully sorted.

q: Insertion sort (ascending) takes each element from the left and inserts it into its place in the sorted part before it. Starting with `[8, 5, 7, 3]`, what is the list just after 7 has been inserted?
x: Insert 5 before 8 → [5, 8, 7, 3]; insert 7 between 5 and 8 → [5, 7, 8, 3]. The 3 is handled in the next step, so it is still last.

q: Binary search on a sorted list with indexes 0 to 10 uses middle index = (low + high) // 2. The target is smaller than the first middle element. Which indexes are still searched?
x: The first middle index is (0 + 10) // 2 = 5. The target is smaller, so high becomes 5 − 1 = 4 and indexes 0 to 4 remain. Keeping index 5 is the classic off-by-one mistake.

q: In the best case, how many comparisons does linear search make to find an item?
x: In the best case the item is the first element, found with 1 comparison. n is the worst case and n / 2 the average.

q: Bubble sort (descending) goes left to right and swaps each adjacent pair whose left value is smaller. What is the list after the first full pass on `[3, 9, 4, 7, 1]`?
x: 3 < 9 swap → [9, 3, 4, 7, 1]; 3 < 4 swap → [9, 4, 3, 7, 1]; 3 < 7 swap → [9, 4, 7, 3, 1]; 3 < 1 no. The smallest value moves to the end; [9, 7, 4, 3, 1] needs more passes.

q: Selection sort sorts a list of 6 elements. How many passes does it need (the last element is in place once the others are)?
x: Each pass places one value; after 5 passes the 5 smallest are in place, so the sixth must already be correct. 15 is the number of comparisons (5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1), not passes.

q: Merge sort splits `[8, 3, 5, 1, 9, 2]` into the halves `[8, 3, 5]` and `[1, 9, 2]`. Just before the final merge, what are the two halves?
x: Each half is sorted on its own: [8, 3, 5] → [3, 5, 8] and [1, 9, 2] → [1, 2, 9]; the final merge then gives [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]. [1, 2, 3] and [5, 8, 9] would mean the values were already mixed between halves, which only the merge does.

q: A stack works on which principle?
x: In a stack the last element pushed is the first one popped, like a pile of plates. FIFO describes a queue.

q: Adding an element at the rear of a queue is called:
x: Enqueue adds at the rear of a queue and dequeue removes from the front. Push and pop are the stack operations.

q: Starting with an empty stack, these operations are done: push 4, push 7, pop, push 2, push 9, pop, push 5. What does the stack hold, from bottom to top?
x: [4] → [4, 7] → pop 7 → [4] → [4, 2] → [4, 2, 9] → pop 9 → [4, 2] → [4, 2, 5]. Read from the top, the same stack is 5, 2, 4, but the question asks bottom to top.

q: Starting with an empty queue: enqueue 3, enqueue 8, enqueue 1, dequeue, enqueue 6, dequeue. Which value is now at the front?
x: [3, 8, 1] → dequeue 3 → [8, 1] → [8, 1, 6] → dequeue 8 → [1, 6], so 1 is at the front. Answering 6 treats the queue like a stack.

q: Starting with an empty stack: push P, push Q, pop, push R, push S, pop, pop. In what order are the values popped?
x: [P, Q] → pop Q → [P] → [P, R, S] → pop S → pop R, leaving [P]. Popping always takes the most recent value, so S comes out before R.

q: The letters of the word CODE are pushed onto an empty stack one at a time, from C to E. All four are then popped. In what order do they come out?
x: E was pushed last, so it is popped first, then D, O and C: the word comes out reversed. C, O, D, E would be the order from a queue.

q:
What is printed?
```
s = []
s.append(3)
s.append(5)
s.append(8)
s.pop()
s.append(1)
print(s)
```
x: `append` adds at the end and `pop()` with no index removes the last item, so the list works as a stack: [3, 5, 8] → [3, 5] → [3, 5, 1]. [5, 8, 1] would mean the first item was removed.

q:
What is printed?
```
q = [10, 20, 30]
q.append(40)
x = q.pop(0)
q.append(x)
print(q)
```
x: [10, 20, 30, 40]; `pop(0)` removes the front item, so x = 10 and q = [20, 30, 40]; appending x gives [20, 30, 40, 10]. [10, 20, 30, 10] forgets that `pop(0)` removes the value as well as returning it.

q: In a binary tree, P is the root; P's left child is Q and right child is R; Q's left child is S and right child is T. What is the in-order traversal (left subtree, node, right subtree)?
x: In-order visits Q's subtree first (S, Q, T), then the root P, then R. P, Q, S, T, R is pre-order and S, T, Q, R, P is post-order.

q: In a binary tree, 50 is the root; 50's left child is 30 and right child is 70; 30's left child is 20 and right child is 40; 70 has only a right child, 80. What is the post-order traversal (left subtree, right subtree, node)?
x: Left subtree of 50 in post-order: 20, 40, 30. Right subtree: 70's only child 80 comes before 70, giving 80, 70. The root 50 is last. Writing 70 before 80 treats 80 as if it were visited after its parent.

q: In a binary tree, M is the root; M's left child is K and right child is T; K has only a right child, L; T has only a left child, R. What is the pre-order traversal (node, left subtree, right subtree)?
x: Pre-order visits M, then K's subtree (K, then its child L), then T's subtree (T, then R). K, L, M, R, T is in-order and M, K, T, L, R is level by level.

q: The values 40, 25, 60, 30, 70 are inserted in that order into an empty binary search tree (smaller values go left, larger go right). Where is 30 placed?
x: 30 < 40, so go left to 25; 30 > 25, so 30 becomes the right child of 25. The right child of 40 is 60, which was inserted earlier.

q: The values 15, 8, 20, 3, 10 are inserted in that order into an empty binary search tree (smaller values go left, larger go right). What is its pre-order traversal (node, left subtree, right subtree)?
x: The tree has root 15, left child 8 (with children 3 and 10) and right child 20. Pre-order gives 15, 8, 3, 10, 20. 3, 8, 10, 15, 20 is the in-order traversal, which is always sorted in a BST.

q: In a tree, a node that has no children is called a:
x: A leaf is a node with no children. The root is the top node with no parent, and an edge is a link between two nodes, not a node.

q: A tree has 7 nodes. How many edges does it have?
x: Every node except the root is joined to its parent by exactly one edge, so a tree with n nodes has n − 1 edges: 7 − 1 = 6.

q: Which statement correctly tells a general graph apart from a tree?
o: A graph has no edges; a tree has edges
A tree may contain cycles; a graph has none
A graph must have a single root node
A graph may contain cycles; a tree has none
x: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles and one root; a general graph may have cycles and has no root. The reversed statement mixes the two up.

q: An undirected graph has vertices P, Q, R, S and edges P–Q, P–R, Q–R and R–S. What is the degree of R?
x: The degree is the number of edges touching a vertex. R appears in P–R, Q–R and R–S, so its degree is 3.

q: An undirected graph has edges P–Q, P–S, Q–R, S–T and R–T. A breadth-first traversal starts at P, uses a queue, and adds unvisited neighbours in alphabetical order. In what order are the vertices visited?
x: From P visit its neighbours Q and S; then Q's unvisited neighbour R; then S's unvisited neighbour T. P, Q, R, T, S is the depth-first order, which goes deep along Q before visiting S.

q: In a singly linked list, what does the "next" link of the last node hold?
o: The address of the first node
The data of the first node
The address of the previous node
x: Each node holds data and a link to the next node; the last node has no next node, so its link is null (`None` in Python). Pointing back to the first node would make a circular list.

q:
What is printed?
```
a = [4, 7, 1]
a.insert(1, 9)
a.remove(7)
print(a)
```
x: `insert(1, 9)` puts 9 at index 1 → [4, 9, 7, 1]; `remove(7)` deletes the value 7 → [4, 9, 1]. [4, 9, 7] would treat `remove` as deleting the last item.

q: Trying to pop an element from an empty stack causes:
x: Removing from an empty stack is underflow. Overflow is pushing onto a stack that is already full.

q: The values 1, 2, 3 are pushed, in that order, onto an empty stack and also enqueued, in that order, into an empty queue. Then one pop and one dequeue are done. Which values are removed?
x: The stack is LIFO, so pop removes the last value pushed, 3. The queue is FIFO, so dequeue removes the first value added, 1.

q: In a binary tree the root alone is level 1, its children are level 2, and so on. What is the largest number of nodes the tree can have in levels 1 to 3?
x: Each node has at most 2 children, so the levels can hold 1, 2 and 4 nodes: 1 + 2 + 4 = 7. 8 is the number of nodes possible on level 4 alone.

q: Print jobs sent to a shared printer are printed in the same order in which they arrive. Which data structure models this?
x: First job in, first job printed is FIFO, which is a queue. A stack would print the newest job first.

q: Which of these is a proposition (a statement that is either true or false)?
x: "Lahore is in Punjab." has a definite truth value (true). A command or a question is not true or false, and x + 2 = 5 depends on x, so it is a predicate, not a proposition.

q: The implication p → q is false only when:
o: p is true and q is false
p is false and q is true
both p and q are false
both p and q are true
x: An implication fails only when the condition holds but the result does not: T → F is false. When p is false, p → q is true whatever q is.

q: In the truth table of p ∧ ¬q (4 rows for p and q), in how many rows is the expression true?
x: p ∧ ¬q needs p true and q false, which happens only in the row p = T, q = F. Every other row makes p false or ¬q false.

q: By De Morgan's law, ¬(p ∧ q) is equivalent to:
x: De Morgan: the negation of an AND is the OR of the negations, so ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q. ¬p ∧ ¬q is the equivalent of ¬(p ∨ q).

q: Which statement is logically equivalent to p → q?
x: The contrapositive ¬q → ¬p has the same truth table as p → q; both are false only when p is true and q is false. The converse q → p and the inverse ¬p → ¬q are false when p is false and q is true, where p → q is true.

q: For which values is (p ∨ q) → r false?
o: p = T, q = F, r = F
p = F, q = F, r = F
p = T, q = T, r = T
p = F, q = T, r = T
x: With p = T, q = F, r = F, p ∨ q is T and r is F, so T → F is false. With p = F, q = F, r = F the condition p ∨ q is false, and F → F is true.

q: Which of these is a tautology (true in every row of its truth table)?
x: If p → q and p are both true, q must be true, so ((p → q) ∧ p) → q is never T → F. (p → q) → (q → p) is false when p = F, q = T (T → F), and so is (p ∨ q) → p.

q: The biconditional p ↔ q is true when:
o: p and q have different truth values
p and q have the same truth value
at least one of p, q is true
x: p ↔ q is true when both are true or both are false. True exactly when they differ is exclusive OR, the negation of ↔.

q: How many rows does the truth table of an expression with three variables p, q and r have?
x: Each variable can be T or F, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 rows. 6 comes from adding 2 + 2 + 2 instead of multiplying.

q: The domain is {1, 2, 3, 4} and P(x) means "x > 2". Which statement is correct?
o: ∃x P(x) and ∀x P(x) are both true
∃x P(x) and ∀x P(x) are both false
∀x P(x) is true and ∃x P(x) is false
∃x P(x) is true and ∀x P(x) is false
x: 3 and 4 are greater than 2, so some x satisfies P(x) and ∃x P(x) is true. 1 and 2 are not, so ∀x P(x) is false.

q: Which is the negation of ∀x P(x)?
x: "Not every x has P" means "some x does not have P": ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x). ∀x ¬P(x) is stronger: it says no x has P.

q: The domain is all students. S(x) means "x studies" and P(x) means "x passes". Which formula says "Every student who studies passes"?
x: "Every … who studies passes" means for every x, if x studies then x passes: ∀x (S(x) → P(x)). ∀x (S(x) ∧ P(x)) would claim every student both studies and passes; ∀x (P(x) → S(x)) reverses the condition.

q:
What is printed?
```
print(not (5 > 3 and 2 > 4))
```
x: 5 > 3 is True and 2 > 4 is False, so the `and` gives False, and `not False` is True. Answering False forgets the `not`.

q: In the truth table of (p ∧ q) ∨ r, with 8 rows for p, q and r, in how many rows is the expression true?
x: When r is true (4 rows) the expression is true. When r is false it needs p ∧ q, which is true in 1 of those 4 rows. Total 4 + 1 = 5.

q: Organising a school sports day is broken into smaller tasks: booking the ground, making the timetable and arranging prizes. Which computational thinking skill is this?
x: Breaking a big problem into smaller parts that can be handled separately is decomposition. Abstraction means leaving out details that do not matter, not splitting the task.

q: A knowledge base has the rule "If it rains, the match is cancelled" and the fact "The match is not cancelled". What can be correctly concluded?
o: The match was played in the rain
x: From p → q and ¬q we conclude ¬p (modus tollens): if it had rained the match would be cancelled, so it did not rain. "Nothing can be concluded" would be right only if the fact were "it did not rain".
